stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: Mar Ukva sent his yearly 400 dinars to a poor neighbor through his son.
stories.turn: The son reported the man did not need it, since they spilled old wine for him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva decided the man was so pampered he needed more, doubled the money and sent it.
stories.summary: Mar Ukva used to send a poor neighbor 400 dinars every Yom Kippur eve. Once his son brought it and came back saying the man did not need it, because he saw them spilling old wine for him. Mar Ukva said that if he is that pampered he needs more, and doubled the gift.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: On his deathbed Mar Ukva asked for his charity records.
stories.turn: He saw he had given seven thousand gold dinars and judged it too little for the long road ahead.
stories.outcome: He gave away half of his remaining wealth to charity.
stories.summary: As Mar Ukva was dying he asked for his charity accounts and found he had given seven thousand gold dinars. Saying his provisions were light and the journey long, he gave away half his money. The Gemara then explains why this did not violate the one-fifth limit.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina and his wife
stories.event: Rabbi Hanina sent his weekly four dinars to a poor man through his wife.
stories.turn: She heard the household asking whether he dined on silver or gold tablecloths and said he did not need charity.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hanina responded by citing Rabbi Elazar that we should be grateful to swindlers.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hanina regularly sent a poor man four dinars before Shabbat. Once his wife delivered it and returned saying the man did not need it, since she heard them ask whether he would dine on silver or gold tablecloths. Rabbi Hanina replied with Rabbi Elazar's saying that swindlers deserve thanks, since without them we would sin daily by neglecting the poor.

stories.actor: A bead seller and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a bead seller for a string, and he asked if she would be betrothed to him with it.
stories.turn: She answered 'Give, give.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled that 'give, give' means nothing; she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man selling glass beads was asked by a woman for a string. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him if he gave it, and she said 'Give, give.' Rav Hama ruled that such an answer is mockery and creates no betrothal.

stories.actor: A man drinking wine and a woman
stories.event: A woman in a wine shop asked a man for a cup, and he asked if she would be betrothed with it.
stories.turn: She replied 'Give me to drink, give me to drink.'
stories.outcome: Rav Hama ruled the reply means nothing and she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man drinking in a store was asked by a woman for a cup of wine. He asked if she would be betrothed to him by it, and she answered 'Give me to drink.' Rav Hama ruled that this answer does not effect betrothal.

stories.actor: A date picker and a woman
stories.event: A woman asked a man picking dates to throw her two, and he asked if she would be betrothed with them.
stories.turn: She said 'Throw, throw.'
stories.outcome: Rav Zevid ruled that this means nothing and she is not betrothed.
stories.summary: A man was picking dates when a woman asked him to throw her two. He asked whether she would be betrothed to him by them, and she said 'Throw, throw.' Rav Zevid ruled that this is not acceptance and she is not betrothed.

stories.actor: A maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household
stories.event: The maidservant immersed and came out of the ritual bath.
stories.turn: A bone was found between her teeth.
stories.outcome: Rabbi required her to immerse again.
stories.summary: A maidservant in Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's household immersed herself, and after she came up a bone was found stuck between her teeth. Rabbi ruled the immersion invalid and required her to immerse again.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Three Sages visiting a place were served a peach as big as a five-se'a stewpot.
stories.turn: A year later Rabbi Elazar came and was given a peach small enough to hold in one hand.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Elazar quoted the verse that a fruitful land becomes salt waste because of its inhabitants' wickedness.
stories.summary: Three Sages came to a certain place and were served an enormous peach; they ate a third, left a third ownerless, and fed a third to their animals. The next year Rabbi Elazar visited and the peach fit in his hand. He cited Psalms: a fruitful land turns to salt waste for the wickedness of its people.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw grape clusters in Gavla as large as calves.
stories.turn: He told the earth to withhold its fruit from the gentiles who ruled them, and the next year the clusters were only the size of goats.
stories.outcome: When Rabbi Hiyya remarked on them, the locals told him to leave and not do what his colleague had done.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi came to Gavla and mistook grape clusters for calves among the vines. Told they were grapes, he called on the earth to gather in its fruit rather than produce it for the gentile rulers. The next year Rabbi Hiyya found clusters the size of goats, and the locals told him to go away and not curse them as his colleague had.

stories.actor: A blind man who studied with Mar Shmuel
stories.event: The blind man was late, so Mar Shmuel sent a messenger to his house, who missed him on the way.
stories.turn: The messenger returned and reported that the blind man's wife had committed adultery.
stories.outcome: Mar Shmuel told him to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and not otherwise.
stories.summary: A blind man who recited mishnayot before Mar Shmuel was late one day, and Mar Shmuel sent a messenger after him. They passed each other, the messenger reached the house and came back saying the man's wife had committed adultery. Mar Shmuel told the blind man to divorce her if he trusted the messenger, and otherwise not to.

stories.actor: King Yannai and Elazar ben Po'ira
stories.event: After conquering sixty cities, King Yannai feasted the Sages on salty food from golden tables.
stories.turn: Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees secretly opposed him and advised testing them with the High Priest's frontplate.
stories.outcome: Yannai stood the Pharisees before him wearing the frontplate (the story continues past the window).
stories.summary: King Yannai returned joyful from conquering sixty cities in Kohalit and summoned the Sages to eat salty foods on golden tables in memory of their ancestors. A scoundrel named Elazar ben Po'ira told him the Pharisees' hearts were against him and suggested he wear the frontplate before them. Yannai did so; the story continues beyond the window.

stories.actor: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: The two Sages seized a dead debtor's boat for themselves and each claimed to have acquired all of it.
stories.turn: Rav Pinehas bar Ami challenged them, and they took the case to Rava.
stories.outcome: Rava rebuked them as white geese stealing cloaks, since seizure after the debtor's death is invalid.
stories.summary: Having told another man's agent his seizure was invalid, Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua seized the boat themselves, one rowing and one pulling, each claiming the whole. Rav Pinehas bar Ami objected that seized goods must lie in the public domain, and they answered they took it from midstream. Rava rebuked them, ruling that seizure counts only while the debtor is alive.

stories.actor: Hama son of Rabba bar Abbahu
stories.event: Hama paid Avimi's debt to the people of Bei Hozai and asked for the loan document back.
stories.turn: They claimed the money was for other, undocumented debts.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu ruled that without witnesses to the payment they could keep both money and document.
stories.summary: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu sent money to his creditors in Bei Hozai through Hama son of Rabba bar Abbahu. After paying, Hama asked for the document, but they said the money covered side debts. Rabbi Abbahu asked whether he had witnesses to the payment; he had none, so the creditors' claim stood.

stories.actor: A woman holding a bag of documents
stories.event: Heirs demanded a bag of documents that had been deposited with a woman.
stories.turn: She claimed she had seized it during the deceased's lifetime for a debt, but had no witnesses.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled it was a seizure after death, which is void.
stories.summary: A woman had a bag of documents deposited with her, and the heirs came to claim it. She said she had seized it while the owner was alive because he owed her money. Rav Nahman asked for witnesses that he demanded it in his lifetime and she refused; she had none, so he ruled the seizure was after death and invalid.

stories.actor: A son sent by his father to fetch chicks
stories.event: At his father's request a son climbed a building, sent away the mother bird and took the chicks.
stories.turn: On his way down he fell.
stories.outcome: He died, despite fulfilling two mitzvot promising long life.
stories.summary: A father told his son to climb up and bring him chicks. The son climbed, sent away the mother bird and took the young, fulfilling both mitzvot whose reward is long life, but fell on his return and died. Rabbi Ya'akov uses this incident to argue the reward refers to the World-to-Come.

stories.actor: Aher (Elisha ben Avuya)
stories.event: Aher saw the tongue of Hutzpit the disseminator dragged in the street by a pig.
stories.turn: He exclaimed: shall a mouth that produced pearls lick the dust?
stories.outcome: He went out and sinned.
stories.summary: Rav Yosef says Aher would not have sinned had he read the verse as Rabbi Ya'akov did; some say he saw a son die after sending away the mother bird. Others say he saw the tongue of the executed Hutzpit the disseminator being dragged by a pig. He cried that a mouth that produced pearls now licks dust, and went out and sinned.

stories.actor: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov
stories.event: Rav Aha found his son's studies weak and went to study with Abaye himself.
stories.turn: Abaye had the townspeople refuse him lodging so he would sleep in the study hall haunted by a demon.
stories.outcome: The demon appeared as a seven-headed serpent; each time Rav Aha bowed in prayer a head fell off, and he survived.
stories.summary: Rav Aha bar Ya'akov sent his son to Abaye, but on his return saw his learning was not sharp, so he decided to go himself. Abaye, hoping for a miracle against a dangerous demon in his study hall, told the townspeople not to host him. Rav Aha slept there, the demon came as a seven-headed serpent, and with each bow of his prayer a head fell off. The next day he told them they had endangered him.

stories.actor: Rav Hamnuna and Rav Huna
stories.event: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna, and Rav Huna asked to meet him.
stories.turn: Rav Huna saw he did not cover his head and learned it was because he was unmarried.
stories.outcome: Rav Huna turned away and told him not to see his face again until he married.
stories.summary: Rav Hisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked to meet him. When Rav Hamnuna came without a head covering, he explained he was not married. Rav Huna turned his face away and told him not to appear before him until he married.

stories.actor: Rabbi Helbo, Rabbi Avira, Rabbi Yosei bar Hanina, and Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Three Sages visiting a place were served an enormous peach.
stories.turn: A year later Rabbi Elazar was given a peach that fit in his hand.
stories.outcome: He quoted the verse that a fruitful land becomes salt waste through its inhabitants' wickedness.
stories.summary: Three Sages came to a certain place and were served a peach the size of a five-se'a stewpot, which they divided among themselves, the public, and their animals. A year later Rabbi Elazar came and the peach was small enough to hold. He cited the verse about a fruitful land turned to salt waste for its people's sins.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi saw grape clusters in Gavla as big as calves.
stories.turn: He told the earth to withhold its fruit from the gentile rulers, and the clusters shrank to the size of goats.
stories.outcome: When Rabbi Hiyya came the next year, the locals told him to leave and not do as his colleague had.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi visited Gavla and mistook huge grape clusters for calves. He told the land to stop producing fruit for the gentiles who ruled over them. The next year Rabbi Hiyya saw clusters like goats, and the locals sent him away so he would not curse them too.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina
stories.event: A red heifer was born in Dama ben Netina's herd as a reward for honoring his father.
stories.turn: The Sages came to buy it, ready to pay any price.
stories.outcome: He asked only for the money he had lost by honoring his father.
stories.summary: The year after Dama ben Netina gave up a profit to honor his father, a red heifer was born in his herd. When the Sages came to buy it, he said he knew they would pay anything. He asked only for the sum he had lost for his father's honor.

stories.actor: Dama ben Netina and his mother
stories.event: Dama ben Netina sat among the nobles of Rome in a golden cloak.
stories.turn: His mother came, tore the cloak off him, struck his head and spat in his face.
stories.outcome: He did not shame her.
stories.summary: Rav Dimi reported that Dama ben Netina once sat among Rome's nobles wearing a gold cloak. His mother came, tore it from him, hit him on the head and spat in his face. Still he did not embarrass her.

stories.actor: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu
stories.event: Avimi, though ordained and with five ordained sons, personally ran to open the door for his father.
stories.turn: Whenever Rabbi Abbahu called at the gate, Avimi called out 'Yes, yes' as he ran.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu held him up as one who properly fulfilled honoring parents (account continues past the window).
stories.summary: Rabbi Abbahu said his son Avimi fulfilled the mitzva of honoring parents. Though Avimi had five ordained sons, when his father called at the gate he ran to open it himself, calling 'Yes, yes' on the way so his father would not feel ignored.

stories.actor: Ravin the Pious
stories.event: Ravin went to betroth a woman to his son.
stories.turn: Her family would not give her to the son, only to him.
stories.outcome: He betrothed her to himself without first telling his son, fearing someone else would take her.
stories.summary: Ravin the Pious went as an agent to betroth a woman for his son but betrothed her to himself. The Gemara explains that her family refused the son and would only give her to Ravin. He did not stop to inform his son because someone else might have betrothed her in the meantime.

stories.actor: Rav and Rabba bar bar Hana
stories.event: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a field for him.
stories.turn: Rav bought it for himself instead.
stories.outcome: The Gemara explains that the violent locals would sell only to Rav, and he feared losing it if he delayed.
stories.summary: Rabba bar bar Hana gave Rav money to buy a certain field for him, but Rav bought it for himself. The field lay among violent men who respected Rav and not Rabba bar bar Hana. Rav did not tell him first, fearing that someone else would buy it meanwhile.

stories.actor: Rav Giddel and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: Rabbi Abba bought a field Rav Giddel had been negotiating for.
stories.turn: Rav Yitzhak Nappaha confronted Rabbi Abba, who said he had not known and offered it as a gift since he would not sell his first land.
stories.outcome: Rav Giddel refused the gift and Rabbi Abba would not use it, so it became known as the land of the Sages.
stories.summary: Rav Giddel was negotiating for a field when Rabbi Abba bought it. Rav Giddel complained to Rabbi Zeira, who took it to Rav Yitzhak Nappaha, and at the Festival he asked Rabbi Abba what happens when someone snatches a pauper's loaf. Rabbi Abba said he had not known and offered the field as a gift, since selling a first purchase is a bad omen. Rav Giddel would not take gifts and Rabbi Abba would not use it, so it was called the land of the Sages.

stories.actor: The family of the woman betrothed with a blue marble stone
stories.event: The family descended from that woman's later marriage remained in Sura.
stories.turn: The Sages suspected the first betrothal might have been valid.
stories.outcome: The Sages refused to marry into the family.
stories.summary: After Rav Hisda invalidated a betrothal made with a blue marble stone, the woman married another man and had descendants in Sura. The Sages kept away from that family, out of concern the children might be mamzerim, following Abaye and Rava's view.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed with a myrtle branch
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman in the marketplace with a myrtle branch.
stories.turn: Rav Aha bar Huna sent the case to Rav Yosef.
stories.outcome: Rav Yosef ruled to flog the man and require a divorce.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman in the market with a myrtle branch. Rav Aha bar Huna asked Rav Yosef what to do. Rav Yosef replied to flog him as Rav would, and require a bill of divorce as Shmuel would, in case the branch was worth a peruta elsewhere.

stories.actor: A son-in-law and Rav Sheshet
stories.event: A son-in-law passed by the door of his father-in-law's house.
stories.turn: There were rumors about him and his mother-in-law.
stories.outcome: Rav Sheshet had him flogged.
stories.summary: A certain son-in-law walked past his father-in-law's door, and Rav Sheshet had him flogged. The Gemara explains that there were suspicions of intimacy between him and his mother-in-law, which his passing fed.

stories.actor: A herdsman of orphans and a creditor
stories.event: A creditor seized an ox from the orphans' herdsman.
stories.turn: The creditor said he seized it in the father's lifetime; the herdsman said after his death; there were no witnesses.
stories.outcome: Rav Nahman ruled for the creditor, since he could have claimed he bought it.
stories.summary: A creditor took an ox from the herdsman of some orphans. The creditor said he seized it while their father was alive, and the herdsman said it was after his death. Rav Nahman found the herdsman had no witnesses and ruled for the creditor, who could as easily have claimed he bought it.

stories.actor: The house of the Nasi and Rabbi Abba
stories.event: The Nasi's household seized a maidservant of orphans in an alley for a debt.
stories.turn: Rabbi Abbahu approved, but Rabbi Abba accused the judges of flattering the Nasi.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abba cited that Reish Lakish reversed such a ruling (window does not say how it ended).
stories.summary: Members of the Nasi's house seized an orphans' maidservant in an alley as payment of their father's debt. Rabbi Abbahu, judging with colleagues, said they had seized well. Rabbi Abba rebuked them for currying favor with the Nasi, noting Reish Lakish had overturned a similar ruling.

stories.actor: Yeimar bar Hashu, Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua
stories.event: Yeimar's agent seized a dead debtor's boat.
stories.turn: Rav Pappa and Rav Huna told him the seizure was invalid and took the boat themselves, each claiming all of it.
stories.outcome: Rava rebuked them as white geese stealing cloaks, since seizure after death does not count.
stories.summary: Yeimar bar Hashu sent his agent to seize a boat left by a debtor who had died. Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua told the agent he could not seize to the detriment of other creditors, then seized it themselves, each claiming the whole. When Rav Pinehas bar Ami objected they said they took it from midstream. Rava called them white geese who strip people's cloaks, since seizure works only during the debtor's life.

stories.actor: Hama son of Rabba bar Abbahu
stories.event: Hama paid Avimi's debt in Bei Hozai and asked for the document.
stories.turn: The creditors said the money was for other debts.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Abbahu ruled that without witnesses he could not recover money or document.
stories.summary: Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu sent payment through Hama, who paid and asked for the loan document. The creditors claimed the payment covered side debts. Rabbi Abbahu ruled that since Hama had no witnesses, the creditors were believed.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed with a bundle of rags
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags.
stories.turn: Rav Shimi bar Hiyya examined whether it was worth a peruta.
stories.outcome: The betrothal depended on whether it had that value.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a bundle of rags. Rav Shimi bar Hiyya, sitting before Rav, examined it to see if it was worth a peruta, ruling the betrothal valid only if it was.

stories.actor: A man who betrothed with a blue marble stone, and his mother
stories.event: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone and Rav Hisda assessed its value.
stories.turn: The man's mother claimed it had been worth a peruta on the day of betrothal.
stories.outcome: Rav Hisda told her she could not make the woman forbidden to a later husband.
stories.summary: A man betrothed a woman with a blue marble stone, and Rav Hisda estimated whether it was worth a peruta. The man's mother said it had been worth that much on the day. Rav Hisda answered that her word could not forbid the woman to someone else.

stories.actor: Yehudit, wife of Rabbi Hiyya
stories.event: Yehudit, suffering painful childbirths, told Rabbi Hiyya her mother said she had been betrothed to another as a child.
stories.turn: This claim would make her forbidden to him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Hiyya said her mother had no power to forbid her to him.
stories.summary: Yehudit, Rabbi Hiyya's wife, had painful childbirths and wanted out of the marriage. She told him her mother said her father had accepted a betrothal for her when she was young. Rabbi Hiyya replied that her mother's word could not make her forbidden to him.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
stories.event: The Angel of Death was sent to do Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's bidding at his death, and he asked to see his place in paradise and to hold the knife.
stories.turn: At paradise he jumped in and swore not to return; God let the oath stand since he had never had an oath annulled.
stories.outcome: He was made to return the knife, Elijah announced him, and he met Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai in paradise.
stories.summary: As Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi was dying, the Angel of Death was told to do his will. He asked to be shown his place in paradise and to hold the knife on the way, then leapt into paradise and swore not to leave. God ruled he could stay, a heavenly voice made him give back the knife, and Elijah proclaimed his arrival. Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai questioned him about rainbows in his day, and out of modesty he said one had been seen.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa
stories.event: When Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa was dying, he asked the Angel of Death for thirty days to review his learning, then for the knife.
stories.turn: The angel refused, suspecting a trick like Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's.
stories.outcome: He died, a pillar of fire separated him from the world, and it withdrew only when Rabbi Alexandri asked in his own honor.
stories.summary: The Angel of Death, his friend, was sent to Rabbi Hanina bar Pappa, who asked for thirty days to review his studies. Afterward he asked to see his place and to hold the knife, but the angel refused, and dismissed his claim of fulfilling the whole Torah. When he died a pillar of fire surrounded him, and it lifted only when Rabbi Alexandri asked it to in his own honor.

stories.actor: An Amorite and a resident of Eretz Yisrael
stories.event: An Amorite asked how many kor of dates a palm on the Jordan bank yields, and was told sixty.
stories.turn: He mocked that the land had been ruined, since they used to pick 120.
stories.outcome: The resident replied that he meant only one side of the tree.
stories.summary: An Amorite asked a resident of Eretz Yisrael how much fruit a palm by the Jordan produced. Told sixty kor, he scoffed that they had ruined the land, since his people got 120. The resident answered that sixty was from one side only.

stories.actor: Rabbi Elazar
stories.event: Rabbi Elazar ascended to Eretz Yisrael and was later ordained and seated in the intercalation council.
stories.turn: At each step he declared he had been spared another curse.
stories.outcome: By the third honor he said he had been spared three (continues past the window).
stories.summary: When Rabbi Elazar went up to Eretz Yisrael he said he had been spared one curse. When ordained he said two, and when seated in the council that sets the calendar, three. The explanation continues beyond the window.

stories.actor: Ameimar
stories.event: While Ameimar judged, a man removed a feather from his head.
stories.turn: The man said he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Ameimar disqualified himself from the case.
stories.summary: A feather landed on Ameimar's head while he sat in judgment, and a man removed it. Asked what he was doing there, the man said he had a case. Ameimar said he was disqualified from judging him.

stories.actor: Mar Ukva
stories.event: A man covered some spittle lying before Mar Ukva.
stories.turn: The man turned out to have a case before him.
stories.outcome: Mar Ukva disqualified himself.
stories.summary: A man covered spittle lying in front of Mar Ukva. When asked his business, he said he had a case. Mar Ukva declared himself unfit to judge it.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei
stories.event: His sharecropper brought the weekly fruit basket on Thursday instead of Friday.
stories.turn: He explained he had a case and brought it on the way.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael refused it, appointed other judges, and found himself still arguing for the man in his mind, and cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei's sharecropper usually brought fruit each Friday, but once came Thursday, saying he had a case that day. Rabbi Yishmael refused the fruit and disqualified himself, seating two scholars to judge. Pacing, he kept thinking of arguments for the sharecropper, and exclaimed that if he was so swayed without taking anything, how much more are those who take bribes.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha
stories.event: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha the first shearing from a distant town.
stories.turn: He admitted he had a case before him.
stories.outcome: Rabbi Yishmael refused it and had others judge, yet still found himself biased, and cursed bribe-takers.
stories.summary: A man brought Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, the first shearing, though there were priests closer to his town. He said he had a case and brought it on the way. Rabbi Yishmael refused, disqualified himself and appointed two scholars, but caught himself rehearsing the man's arguments and declared how much worse it must be for those who accept bribes.

stories.actor: Rav Anan
stories.event: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of small fish and said he had a case.
stories.turn: Rav Anan refused, but the man said he wanted no judgment, only to give a gift like first fruits.
stories.outcome: Rav Anan accepted it and sent him to Rav Nahman with a note that he was disqualified (continues past the window).
stories.summary: A man brought Rav Anan a basket of fish, and when he mentioned a case Rav Anan refused it. The man said he no longer wanted Rav Anan's judgment, only to give a scholar a gift, which is like bringing first fruits. Rav Anan accepted and sent him to Rav Nahman saying he was disqualified; Rav Nahman assumed the man was a relative and began to defer an orphans' case.

stories.actor: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's son
stories.event: Rabbi arranged his son's marriage into the house of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, with twelve years of study first.
stories.turn: Seeing the bride, the son shortened it to six years, then married at once and was ashamed before his father.
stories.outcome: After twelve years' study his wife had become infertile; he prayed and she was healed.
stories.summary: A son was matched with a daughter of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra's household, to study twelve years first. When she was shown to him he cut it to six, then decided to marry first, and was embarrassed before his father, who reassured him that God too moved up His plans. He then studied twelve years and returned to find his wife infertile; he prayed for her and she was cured.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai
stories.event: Rabbi Hananya left for twelve years of study and returned to find his town's paths changed.
stories.turn: He followed a girl called 'daughter of Hakhinai' home, and his wife died of shock on seeing him.
stories.outcome: He prayed and she was revived.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai left for the study hall without waiting for Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai and stayed twelve years. Returning, he could not find his house, but heard a girl called daughter of Hakhinai and followed her. His wife, sifting flour, looked up, saw him, and died from shock. He pleaded with God and she lived.

stories.actor: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa
stories.event: After twelve years of study, Rabbi Hama sent word home rather than surprising his wife.
stories.turn: A sharp young scholar questioned him and he regretted not having such a son, not knowing it was his son Oshaya.
stories.outcome: At home he stood up for the young man, and his wife told him a father does not stand for his son.
stories.summary: Rabbi Hama bar Bisa studied twelve years and, to avoid Ben Hakhinai's mistake, waited in the local study hall and sent word home. A brilliant young man questioned him, and he lamented that had he stayed home he might have such a son. When the young man followed him home and he rose in his honor, his wife asked whether a father stands for his son: it was his son Rabbi Oshaya.

stories.actor: Rabbi Akiva and Ben Kalba Savua's daughter
stories.event: Ben Kalba Savua's daughter secretly betrothed herself to his shepherd Akiva on condition he study.
stories.turn: Her father expelled her and vowed she would not benefit from his property.
stories.outcome: Akiva studied twelve years and returned with twelve thousand students (story continues past the window).
stories.summary: Rabbi Akiva was the shepherd of the wealthy Ben Kalba Savua, whose daughter saw his fine character and offered to marry him if he would study Torah. They betrothed secretly and she sent him off; her father threw her out and disinherited her. After twelve years Akiva returned with twelve thousand students and overheard an old man speaking to his wife; the story continues beyond the window.

stories.actor: Rav Huna and his son Rabba
stories.event: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son to test him.
stories.turn: He wanted to see whether Rabba would grow angry.
stories.outcome: The Gemara explains he had waived his honor and tore at the seam.
stories.summary: Rav Huna tore silk garments in front of his son Rabba to see whether he would become angry. The Gemara discusses whether this caused his son to stumble or wasted property, and explains that he had forgone his honor and tore only at a seam.

stories.actor: Rav Yehezkel and his sons
stories.event: Rav Yehezkel taught his son Rami a law about mixing condemned people.
stories.turn: His other son Rav Yehuda told him not to teach it that way and corrected the wording.
stories.outcome: Rav Yehuda proposed the reversed version (continues past the window).
stories.summary: Rav Yehezkel was teaching his son Rami that when those sentenced to burning are mixed with those sentenced to stoning, all are stoned. His other son Rav Yehuda objected, 'Father, do not teach it this way,' because majority alone would explain it. He offered the reversed wording instead.

stories.actor: The people of Bireta DeSatya
stories.event: A ditch overflowed with fish and the townspeople trapped them on Shabbat.
stories.turn: Rabbi Ahai son of Rabbi Yoshiya excommunicated them.
stories.outcome: They all abandoned Judaism, as Rabbi foresaw on his deathbed.
stories.summary: On his deathbed Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi declared that the people of Bireta DeSatya had that day turned from God. A ditch had overflowed with fish and they caught them on Shabbat. Rabbi Ahai son of Rabbi Yoshiya excommunicated them, and they apostatized.

stories.actor: Pelatiah son of Benaiah
stories.event: Nebuchadnezzar's son-in-law asked for captives to serve him, and Nebuchadnezzar planned to send Jews.
stories.turn: Pelatiah advised Nebuchadnezzar to keep the nobles himself and send the servants instead.
stories.outcome: Ezekiel lamented that one who did good for Israel should die in mid-life.
stories.summary: Nebuchadnezzar's son-in-law, governor of Meishan, complained he had been sent no captives to serve him. Nebuchadnezzar meant to send Jews, but Pelatiah son of Benaiah suggested the important Jews stay to serve the king and their slaves go instead. When Pelatiah died, Ezekiel cried out that one who did Israel this good should die halfway through his days.
